strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper provides a principled formulation of sequential Bayesian experimental design for LLM-based information gathering, and convincingly identifies a key flaw in prior work (implicit reduction of EIG to marginal predictive entropy when assuming constant expected likelihood entropy).

Careful and thorough treatment of design decisions, including the prior–likelihood vs. data–estimation pairings, belief updating via sample-then-filter rejection sampling, and candidate question generation; the theoretical discussion in Section 4 (faithfulness of conditional distributions, alignment between EIG and the actual update procedure) adds genuine insight beyond a recipe.

Strong and consistent empirical results: BED-LLM outperforms carefully controlled Entropy and Naive QA baselines across 5 LLMs, 3 datasets (e.g., 14% to 91% success on Celebrities with Mistral-Large), with large margins; results hold under model misspecification (different questioner/answerer LLMs).

Good ablations: the data–estimation pairing ablation directly supports the central design claim, and the per-turn analysis (Figure 2) plus EIG-progression analysis (Appendix E.1) help explain when and why the method helps.
Well-controlled baseline: the Entropy baseline shares prompts, candidate generation, and filtering with BED-LLM, isolating the effect of the EIG estimator rather than other engineering choices.
Clear writing and honest positioning; the paper is transparent about limitations of direct comparison to prior work (e.g., footnote 5) and about where the approach applies.
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely with LLM-simulated users/answerers; no human-subject validation, so it is unclear whether the reported gains transfer to real users whose response distributions may deviate substantially from LLM answerers—the very setting motivating the work.

Task scope is narrow: only two settings (20-Questions and movie preference elicitation), and both are restricted to multiple-choice questions with small response spaces; the claimed generality (diagnosis, tutoring, surveys, scientific discovery) is asserted but not tested.

Evaluation of preference elicitation relies on LLM-as-judge ratings conditioned on an oracle LLM-generated persona, which is a weak and potentially biased proxy for recommendation quality; the o3-generated personas and Animals dataset also introduce possible distributional artifacts.

Several important components are heuristic with limited sensitivity analysis in the main text: filtering likelihood threshold, temperature T=1.3, N=15 hypotheses, M=15/8 candidates, hypothesis-retention policy; the method's sensitivity to these choices is not systematically quantified.

Computational cost is not well characterized; the method requires many LLM calls per turn (hypothesis generation/filtering plus likelihood evaluations per candidate question), and the cost-performance trade-off relative to simpler baselines is not reported.

Lack of direct comparison with prior EIG-style methods (due to unavailable code/setups) means the claims of superiority over specific prior systems rest partly on re-implemented approximations rather than head-to-head results.

The sequential/myopic nature of the approach (no lookahead planning) is acknowledged as suboptimal, and the paper offers only discussion (Appendix A.3) rather than mitigation or empirical characterization of this limitation.

strengths: Principled and clearly articulated application of sequential Bayesian experimental design to LLM-driven information gathering, with a careful analysis of the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing and when each is appropriate.

Strong empirical gains on 20-Questions (e.g., 14% to 91% on Celebrities with Mistral-Large), consistently outperforming both the Entropy and Naive QA baselines across five different LLMs and three datasets.

Well-designed ablations: the Entropy baseline is kept as close to BED-LLM as possible (same prompts, candidate generation, hypothesis filtering), isolating the contribution of the full EIG estimator; the data-estimation ablation and misspecification (different questioner/answerer LLM) experiments are valuable.

Useful identification that prior work (Kobalczyk et al. 2025, Mazzaccara et al. 2024, Cooper et al. 2025) implicitly reduces EIG to marginal predictive entropy, and demonstration that this degrades performance, especially as history grows.
Detailed appendix providing implementation specifics (hypothesis generation, prompts, filtering thresholds, datasets) that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: All evaluation uses LLM-simulated answerers; there are no experiments with real human participants. Given the paper's central claim is about improving interactive information gathering from users, the extent to which conclusions transfer to human answerers (whose responses may be noisier, inconsistent, or adversarial) remains unverified.

No reporting of computational cost. BED-LLM requires generating N hypotheses, filtering each against the history, and computing likelihoods for M candidate questions each turn, plus guess extraction. The paper should quantify the LLM-call/token overhead relative to the Naive QA baseline and discuss when this is worth it.

Fairness of the comparison is partially confounded: the Entropy baseline shares BED-LLM's hypothesis-generation and filtering machinery, so some of the gap between Naive QA and Entropy may come from this shared scaffolding rather than from the acquisition function. The paper's claim that its Entropy baseline is stronger than prior published methods actually suggests prior comparisons in the literature were weaker than implied here.

Heavy reliance on engineering heuristics whose sensitivity is not fully ablated: temperature T=1.3, filtering likelihood thresholds, N=15/M=15 candidate counts, hypothesis-retention, context reordering, and prompt wording. The paper itself concedes 'the precise prompting strategy... can also be quite important', which weakens the generality claim.

Scope is narrow: only multiple-choice/yes-no queries are supported, and only two task families (20-Questions, movie preference elicitation) are evaluated. The broad applicability suggested in Sections 2-4 (code clarification, diagnosis, tutoring, document retrieval) is not empirically demonstrated.

The preference elicitation evaluation uses LLM-as-judge ratings derived from personas generated by o3 from MovieLens ratings, an indirect and noisy proxy for true user preference; gains over baselines are small and only emerge by turn 3, and error bars show substantial overlap in several configurations.

Termination and guessing mechanics (e.g., asking 'Is it <item>?' when hypotheses collapse) introduce design choices specific to 20-Questions that may not generalize to other information-gathering settings.
Some positioning claims are hard to fully verify given limited detail available from compared prior work (footnote 5 relies on rebuttal statements from OpenReview rather than direct reproduction).

strengths: The paper formulates interactive information gathering with LLMs as sequential Bayesian experimental design in a principled way, and provides an unusually thorough analysis of key design decisions (prior–likelihood vs. data–estimation pairings, alignment between EIG formulation and belief updating in Section 4), which is a genuine contribution beyond prior heuristic or entropy-based approaches.

The central empirical claim—that previous prior–likelihood BED methods implicitly reduce to predictive entropy and that the full EIG estimator matters—is well motivated (Section 3.2.1, Figure 1) and validated: the strong 'Entropy' baseline uses the same prompts, candidate generation, and filtering, isolating the EIG contribution cleanly.

Results are convincing and extensive: substantial gains across 3 datasets (20–Questions) and 5 LLMs (e.g., 14%→91% on Celebrities with Mistral-Large), with per-turn curves, cross-model (questioner/answerer misspecification) experiments, and a data–estimation ablation that empirically supports the theoretical analysis in Section 4.

The belief-updating procedure (sample–then–filter with hypothesis retention) is a sensible and well-justified response to documented in-context learning failures, supported by diagnostic evidence (Figure 8) of LLM prior over-collapsing.
The paper is honest about limitations, e.g., the footnote on inability to compare directly with Kobalczyk et al. (2025), and the discussion of when the data–estimation pairing would be preferable.
weaknesses: All evaluation uses LLM-simulated answerers rather than real humans, which is a significant concern for a paper about eliciting information from users. In the same-model condition there is potential circularity: the questioner's likelihood model may align well with the simulator's response distribution, inflating gains for model-based methods. The cross-model experiments mitigate but do not eliminate this concern, and the preference-elicitation task (arguably the most human-relevant) shows only modest gains over baselines.

Scope is narrow: two question-asking tasks, both involving multiple-choice/Yes-No queries. The claim of a 'general-purpose approach' is stronger than the evidence; settings involving free-form responses, tool calls, or retrieval (mentioned in the introduction) are untested.

No analysis of computational cost: BED-LLM requires many LLM calls per turn (hypothesis sampling/filtering, M candidate questions × N hypotheses likelihood evaluations), yet no wall-clock, token-budget, or accuracy-per-cost comparison is provided against Naive QA, which is orders of magnitude cheaper.

Several components are effectively prompt-engineering heuristics (filtering thresholds, hypothesis retention, batched 'diverse' generation, T=1.3, context reordering), with limited sensitivity analysis or ablations over N, M, and the filtering threshold, weakening reproducibility and generality claims.

No direct head-to-head comparison with any prior published method's actual system; comparisons are to re-implemented variants (Entropy, Naive QA, Data–Estimation) within the authors' own framework, and reliance on OpenReview statements for claims about Kobalczyk et al. is not ideal.
The theoretical treatment in Section 4 is informal and the estimator is biased for finite N with small N=15; the practical impact of this bias on question ranking is not quantified.

The preference-elicitation evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge scoring by the same answerer LLM conditioned on θ*, introducing possible evaluator bias and correlation with the persona used in the dialogue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem—adaptive multi-turn information gathering with LLMs—where prior work has documented clear LLM failures (e.g., multi-turn guessing games, clarification questions), and the proposed BED-LLM framework is a principled and well-motivated solution.

The technical treatment is unusually careful and thorough for an LLM-systems paper: the discussion of prior–likelihood vs. data–estimation pairings (§4, §B), the Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator, the argument against deterministic-likelihood assumptions (§3.2, §A.2), and the alignment of the EIG objective with the actual belief-updating procedure (§B.3) provide genuine conceptual insight, not just an engineering recipe.

The evaluation is comprehensive: three 20 Questions datasets, four LLMs, questioner–answerer mismatch settings, a second task (preference elicitation) where θ is abstract and the deterministic-likelihood baseline is inapplicable, and four targeted ablations (Entropy, Data–Estimation, ICL Beliefs, Implicit Maximization) that isolate each algorithmic component and empirically validate the theoretical claims in §4.

Baselines appear strong: the authors report that their own Split implementation substantially outperforms numbers previously reported in the literature (e.g., Kobalczyk et al., 2025), so BED-LLM's gains are measured against a strengthened state-of-the-art rather than a strawman.
Hypothesis-space openness (the target set is never given to the questioner) is a more demanding and realistic setting than much prior work that relied on pre-enumerated finite candidate sets.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed algorithmic descriptions, full prompts (Figs. 4–10), and explicit hyperparameter reporting in appendices.
weaknesses: All evaluation relies on an LLM answerer simulating user responses, and preference-elicitation ratings are produced by LLM-as-judge using the same answerer model conditioned on θ*, introducing potential circularity; no experiments with real human responders are included, so claims of applicability to real users rest on the mismatch experiments alone.

The baselines outside the authors' own ablations are limited: essentially only Naive and Split (with Split inapplicable to preference elicitation). Head-to-head numbers against the actual published implementations of Hu et al. (2024), Kobalczyk et al. (2025), or Zhang et al. (2024) on their original benchmarks are not provided.

Computational cost is a significant practical concern—the approach requires sampling many hypotheses and questions plus likelihood evaluations per turn, per candidate—and while a claim is made that the entropy ablation requires the same LLM calls, no overall wall-clock/token-cost comparison versus Naive/Split is reported.

Several design choices are fixed without sensitivity analysis: the rejection threshold (0.2), number of hypotheses (N=15) and questions (M=15), the uniform prior over filtered candidates, and the temperature/diversity prompting heuristics; robustness of the gains to these choices is unverified.

The preference-elicitation evaluation metric (mean LLM-judge rating over 5 turns, final mean ~4.0–4.5) shows smaller and less consistent gains than 20 Questions, and its statistical significance is not tested; the restriction to multiple-choice questions may also limit generality.

Some novelty framing is slightly overstated—the core idea of EIG-based question selection for LLMs exists in several prior works (which the authors acknowledge as variants of Split); the contribution is more a principled refinement than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Terminological inconsistencies (e.g., the '5.8x gain' for Llama-3.1-8B appears inconsistent with Table 1 numbers; 'valid samples' wording in §E) and occasional overreach in the abstract/conclusion slightly weaken the presentation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: LLMs struggle to adaptively gather information across multi-turn interactions, and the proposed BED-LLM framework is a principled deployment-time solution that requires no fine-tuning and applies to any LLM.

The methodological analysis is unusually careful and thorough: the discussion of prior–likelihood vs. data–estimation pairings (§4, §B), the argument against deterministic-likelihood assumptions that collapse EIG to marginal predictive entropy (§3.2, §A.2.1), and the alignment between the EIG objective and the belief-updating procedure (§B.3) provide genuine conceptual insight beyond prior ad hoc EIG-based LLM methods.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive: three 20 Questions problem sets across five LLMs, cross-model questioner/answerer settings testing robustness to model misspecification, a second task domain (preference elicitation), and four well-designed ablations (Entropy, Data-Estimation, ICL Beliefs, Implicit Maximization) that each isolate a specific design decision. The gains over the strengthened Naive and Split baselines are large (e.g., 5.8x for Llama-3.1-8B) and consistent.

The paper is honest about baseline strength — the authors note their Split implementation dramatically outperforms previously reported results, making the comparison more convincing — and the ablations convincingly attribute gains to the full EIG objective and the hypothesis filtering mechanism rather than to extra compute alone.
The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: prompts, hyperparameters (N, M, temperature, filtering threshold), problem sets, and evaluation protocols are all documented.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies entirely on LLM-simulated answerers and LLM-as-judge scoring for preference elicitation; there is no evaluation with real human users, which weakens the central claim of applicability to genuine interactive information gathering. The preference-elicitation results in particular rest on a single judge model whose biases are unquantified.

Several components of the method are heuristic and under-justified despite the 'principled' framing: the fixed likelihood-filter threshold of 0.2, the uniform prior imposed over filtered hypotheses, the ad hoc diversity-encouraging prompts, temperature T=1.3, and the hypothesis-retention mechanism. No sensitivity analysis or ablation of these hyperparameters is provided, so it is hard to know how much of the gain depends on brittle prompt/tuning choices.

The computational cost of BED-LLM is substantial (sampling and filtering many hypotheses, computing EIG for M candidate questions with N posterior samples per turn) but is never quantified in terms of tokens, wall-clock time, or cost, making it difficult to judge practicality relative to the much cheaper Naive baseline.

The theoretical framing is loose: the belief update pf(θ; ht−1) is not Bayesian, the estimator's claimed convergence under 'decaying correlation' is asserted rather than analyzed, and the discussion in §4/§B.3 about when prior–likelihood should be preferred is largely qualitative and validated only on tasks where the authors' preferred formulation happens to win.

Scope is narrow in practice: questions are restricted to multiple-choice format to make entropies tractable, which limits the claimed generality to 'retrieving documents or calling external functions'; no experiment demonstrates these broader query types. Only two task domains are tested, both fairly benign.

Some claims of firsts (e.g., 'first work to use this prior–likelihood pairing without a deterministic likelihood assumption') are narrow distinctions relative to closely related concurrent work (e.g., Wang et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2025), and the incremental novelty over the strong Split-style prior methods, while real, may be smaller than the presentation suggests.

strengths: Principled and clearly articulated formulation of LLM-driven information gathering as sequential Bayesian experimental design, with a genuinely careful treatment of how the joint model p(θ, y; x) should be constructed from an LLM (prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing) — an analysis largely missing from prior work.

The avoidance of the deterministic-likelihood assumption (which reduces EIG to marginal predictive entropy in most prior methods) is a meaningful technical contribution, well-motivated both theoretically (§3.2, §A.2) and empirically (Entropy ablation).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 20 Questions across three datasets and five LLMs plus questioner-answerer mismatch settings, and a preference-elicitation task with a different (abstract, open-ended) hypothesis space; results show consistent and often large gains (e.g., ~5.8x for Llama-3.1-8B on Celebrities).

Thoughtful ablation suite (Entropy, Data-Estimation, ICL Beliefs, Implicit Maximization) that cleanly isolates the contribution of each algorithmic component, and the ablation results directly validate the paper's theoretical claims about pairing choice and filtering.

Baselines appear to be strengthened relative to prior reports (the Split implementation outperforms numbers in Kobalczyk et al. 2025), which makes the comparison more convincing rather than less; the unrestricted (non-closed-world) hypothesis space is also more realistic than in much prior work.

Appendices provide substantial design analysis (alignment of EIG with belief updating via expected uncertainty reduction, choice of θ, likelihood updating), supporting reproducibility and giving the community reusable insights; detailed prompts and hyperparameters are reported.
weaknesses: Both experiments use simulated users (an answerer LLM prompted with the ground truth), and the preference-elicitation evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge where the judge is the answerer model itself — this introduces potential circularity/bias and leaves open how well gains transfer to real human users, which is the paper's stated motivating application.

Scope is limited to two task types (multiple-choice 20 Questions and film preference elicitation); the claimed generality of the 'general-purpose approach' (e.g., tool use, retrieval, clarification) is not empirically demonstrated.

Several design choices are heuristic and not ablated: the 0.2 likelihood filtering threshold, uniform prior over filtered hypotheses, M=15/N=15 sample sizes, and temperature settings; sensitivity to these is not reported.

Computational cost is not systematically reported; BED-LLM requires many more LLM calls per turn than Naive/Split baselines (hypothesis sampling, filtering, EIG estimation over M candidates × N samples), and the accuracy-per-compute trade-off is not characterized.
The approach is myopic (greedy incremental EIG), which the authors acknowledge is potentially suboptimal for sequential settings; no comparison to or discussion of how much this costs in practice.

Some theoretical claims (e.g., that pf is 'better approximated by a Bayesian update') are argued qualitatively rather than tested directly; the Rao-Blackwellization claim assumes the LLM's predictive distribution is a reasonable calibrated likelihood, which the paper itself concedes is often not the case in θ-space.

Minor issues: the evaluation-guess mechanism ('Is it ⟨item⟩?' when hypotheses collapse) partially entangles the guessing strategy with question-selection performance; some typos and undefined notation early in §4 ('p (yt; [ht-1, xt])' before full definition).
